title: Bitwise Operators
summary: Work with the bits of an integer, and store yes or no flags in one column.
intro: An integer is a row of bits, and PostgreSQL has operators that work on those bits one at a time. That lets one `integer` column hold several yes or no flags, like the read, write, delete, and admin permissions of a user.
setup:
CREATE TABLE users (id integer, name text, perms integer);
INSERT INTO users (id, name, perms) VALUES
    (1, 'Ana', 15),
    (2, 'Ben', 3),
    (3, 'Cara', 1),
    (4, 'Dev', 7),
    (5, 'Eli', 5),
    (6, 'Fay', 0);

steps.title: Bits and operators
steps.body:
Every integer is stored as bits: 12 is `1100` and 10 is `1010`. Cast to `bit(n)` to see the last `n` bits: `12::bit(4)` prints `1100`.

These operators compare two numbers bit by bit:

| Operator | Keeps a 1 where | `12 op 10` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `&` and | both bits are 1 | 8 (`1000`) |
| `\|` or | either bit is 1 | 14 (`1110`) |
| `#` xor | exactly one bit is 1 | 6 (`0110`) |

`~` flips every bit of one number. `<<` shifts bits left and `>>` shifts them right, so `1 << 3` is 8 and `16 >> 2` is 4. Each left shift doubles the number.

```sql
SELECT ~5 AS not_five, 1 << 3 AS eight, 16 >> 2 AS four;
```

Gotchas:

- Xor is `#`, not `^`. In PostgreSQL `2 ^ 3` is 8, a power.
- `~5` is `-6`, not `2`: all 32 bits flip, leading zeros included. Between two values `~` is still the regex match.
- `&`, `|`, `#`, `<<`, and `>>` share one precedence and run left to right, so `1 | 2 & 4` is `(1 | 2) & 4`, which is 0. Use parentheses.
- `::` binds tighter than all of them, so wrap a result to cast it: `(12 & 10)::bit(4)`.

example.title: Twelve and ten
example.prompt: Combine 12 and 10 with and, or, and xor, show both as 4 bits, and shift 1 left by 3.
example.code: SELECT 12 & 10 AS and_bits, 12 | 10 AS or_bits, 12 # 10 AS xor_bits, 12::bit(4) AS twelve, 10::bit(4) AS ten, 1 << 3 AS shifted;
example.explanation: `1100 & 1010` keeps only the first bit, which both share, so it is `1000`, or 8. Or keeps any bit that is set in either, `1110` or 14. Xor keeps the bits that differ, `0110` or 6. `1 << 3` moves the single 1 three places left: `1000`, which is 8.

practice.title: Nine and five
practice.prompt:
Build the same row of bitwise results for 9 and 5.

1. Select `9 & 5` as `and_bits`, `9 | 5` as `or_bits`, and `9 # 5` as `xor_bits`.
2. Show 9 and 5 as 4 bits, named `nine` and `five`.
3. Shift 40 right by 2, named `shifted`.

Expected output:

```text
 and_bits | or_bits | xor_bits | nine | five | shifted
----------+---------+----------+------+------+---------
        1 |      13 |       12 | 1001 | 0101 |      10
(1 row)
```
practice.starter:
-- TODO: replace the zeros with bitwise expressions, then add nine, five, and shifted
SELECT 0 AS and_bits, 0 AS or_bits, 0 AS xor_bits;
practice.solution: SELECT 9 & 5 AS and_bits, 9 | 5 AS or_bits, 9 # 5 AS xor_bits, 9::bit(4) AS nine, 5::bit(4) AS five, 40 >> 2 AS shifted;
hints: Copy the shape of the example and swap 12 and 10 for 9 and 5.
Xor is `#`, and a cast like `9::bit(4)` shows the bits.
`>>` moves bits right, and each step right halves the number.

steps.title: Flags in one column
steps.body:
The `users` table stores each user's permissions in one integer, one bit per yes or no flag: 1 = read, 2 = write, 4 = delete, 8 = admin. A user's value is the sum of their flags, so read and write together is 1 + 2, which is 3.

```sql harness
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS users CASCADE;
{{code}}
```

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (id integer, name text, perms integer);
```

```text
 id | name | perms
----+------+-------
  1 | Ana  |    15
  2 | Ben  |     3
  3 | Cara |     1
```

Three moves cover almost everything:

- **Test** a flag with `&`: `(perms & 4) <> 0` is true when the delete bit is on.
- **Set** a flag with `|`: `perms | 4` turns delete on and leaves the rest alone. Setting it twice changes nothing.
- **Clear** a flag with `& ~`: `perms & ~4` keeps every bit except delete.

Write the test as `(perms & 4) <> 0` with parentheses. It works without them, but the parentheses make it read clearly. Avoid `+` and `-` to change flags: `perms + 4` breaks a user who already has delete, and `perms - 2` breaks one without write. `|` and `& ~` are always safe.

example.title: Who can write
example.prompt: For every user, show the bits, whether they can write, their perms with delete added, and their perms with write removed.
example.code:
SELECT
    name,
    perms::bit(4) AS bits,
    (perms & 2) <> 0 AS can_write,
    perms | 4 AS with_delete,
    perms & ~2 AS without_write
FROM users
ORDER BY id;
example.explanation: `perms::bit(4)` shows the four flags, with admin on the left and read on the right. `perms & 2` is 2 when the write bit is on and 0 when it is off, so comparing it with 0 gives a boolean. `perms | 4` sets delete, so Dev and Eli, who already had it, keep the same number. `perms & ~2` clears write, which leaves Cara, Eli, and Fay unchanged.

practice.title: Promote or demote the deleters
practice.prompt:
List the users who can delete, with their permissions after you make them admins, and after you take delete away instead.

1. Select `name` from `users`.
2. Add `perms` with the admin flag (8) set, named `with_admin`, and the same value as 4 bits, named `new_bits`.
3. Add `perms` with the delete flag (4) cleared, named `without_delete`.
4. Keep only the users whose delete flag (4) is on.
5. Sort by `id`.

Expected output:

```text
 name | with_admin | new_bits | without_delete
------+------------+----------+----------------
 Ana  |         15 | 1111     |             11
 Dev  |         15 | 1111     |              3
 Eli  |         13 | 1101     |              1
(3 rows)
```
practice.starter:
SELECT name, perms
FROM users
-- TODO: keep only users who can delete, and add with_admin, new_bits, and without_delete
ORDER BY id;
practice.solution:
SELECT
    name,
    perms | 8 AS with_admin,
    (perms | 8)::bit(4) AS new_bits,
    perms & ~4 AS without_delete
FROM users
WHERE (perms & 4) <> 0
ORDER BY id;

tests.stdin: UPDATE users SET perms = 4 WHERE id = 6; INSERT INTO users (id, name, perms) VALUES (7, 'Gus', 12), (8, 'Hana', 10);

hints: Filter in `WHERE` with the test move from the body, using the delete flag 4.
`|` sets a flag and `& ~` clears one, without touching the others. Use 8 for `with_admin` and 4 for `without_delete`.
`::` binds tighter than `|`, so put parentheses around the expression before you cast it to `bit(4)`.

recap:
- `&` keeps bits set in both, `|` bits set in either, `#` bits set in one only. Xor is `#` because `^` is a power.
- `~` flips every bit, and `<<` and `>>` shift bits left and right.
- `n::bit(4)` shows the last 4 bits of a number.
- One integer can hold many yes or no flags, one bit each.
- Test a flag with `(perms & 4) <> 0`, set it with `perms | 4`, and clear it with `perms & ~4`.
